title: "Instructor notes"
---

Not for students. Keep this page out of the handout you hand out, or delete it
from `_quarto.yml` before publishing.

## Timing

| Part | Format | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 0 · Setup | **homework, before class** | 20 min |
| 1 · Four ideas | lecture + napkin check | 15 min |
| 2 · Solo walkthrough | live demo, then they do it | 40 min |
| 3 · Collaboration cycle | in groups, one PR each | 45 min |
| 3 · Conflict, on purpose | **scripted, whole class together** | 30 min |
| 3½ · Conflict on a pull request | scripted, in pairs | 20 min |
| 4–5 · Troubleshooting, rules | read + discuss | 15 min |

Two sessions of 90 minutes, or one long workshop. Part 0 as homework is not
optional — doing installs and OAuth in class will consume the entire session
and half the students will still be stuck.

## Check before the session

Ask every student to paste the output of these four commands into the course
forum a few days before:

```bash
git --version
gh auth status
git config --global --list | grep -E "user\.|defaultBranch|rebase"
R --version
```

The failure you will see most is a missing `pull.rebase`. It does not break
anything until two people diverge — that is, precisely during the group
exercise — and then it fails hard with a wall of hints. Catch it early.

## Running the conflict exercise

Do not hope a conflict happens. Script it:

1. Pair the students. Both pull `main`.
2. Both open `report.qmd` and write a paragraph in the **Interpretation**
   section — the same lines, their own words.
3. **Student C pushes first.** Fine.
4. **Student A pushes.** Rejected. *Stop here and read the hint together as a
   class* — this is the single most valuable 60 seconds of the session.
5. Student A pulls → conflict.
6. Resolve **by hand first**, so everyone has seen the markers in a real file.
7. *Then* re-run it and resolve with a prompt, so they see the difference.

The pedagogical payload is step 4, not step 5. The rejected push is the moment
they understand that git is protecting the other person.

## Running the Part 3½ exercise

Do this *after* Part 3, because the contrast is the lesson: in Part 3 the push
is rejected, here it succeeds and GitHub complains later. Students who only see
one of the two conclude the wrong general rule.

To engineer it reliably, in pairs:

1. Both pull `main`.
2. **Student A** branches (`feature/limitations`) and edits the closing lines of
   the Interpretation section. Does *not* push yet.
3. **Student C** edits the *same* lines and gets them onto `main` — in class,
   pushing straight to `main` is the quickest way; in their real project this
   happens because C's PR was merged.
4. A pushes the branch — **it succeeds**. Pause here and ask the class whether
   everything is fine. Most will say yes.
5. A opens the PR. `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus` →
   `CONFLICTING / DIRTY`.
6. A fixes it with `git merge origin/main` *inside the branch*, resolves,
   renders, pushes. The PR flips to `MERGEABLE / CLEAN`.

Two points worth labouring:

- **Direction.** Merging their branch into `main` locally would "work" and
  would bypass review entirely. Ask them why that is bad before you tell them.
- **Asymmetry.** Here `HEAD` is their unreviewed branch and the other side is
  merged, accepted work. The Part 3 instinct of "combine both equally" can
  silently reverse a group decision inside a merge commit, where no reviewer
  will ever see it.

`mergeable: UNKNOWN` right after a push is normal — GitHub computes it
asynchronously. Tell them in advance or you will field the question five times.

## Why the example project is shaped this way

**Owner-per-file plus one shared section.** Their real group work should flow
without conflicts; the shared `Interpretation` section is the designated safe
place to learn the skill.

**Simulated data with a known effect (arm effect = −4).** The model recovers
−5.23 (95% CI −7.53 to −2.94). The interval covers the truth and the point
estimate misses it by 1.2. Almost no real dataset lets students see sampling
variation against a known answer, so this is worth a detour even though the
course is about git. It also makes the conflict resolution substantive: the two
paragraphs disagree about *what to emphasise*, not about facts.

**The 4 KB CSV is committed on purpose.** "Never commit data" is the usual
advice and it is wrong often enough to be harmful — students who follow it
literally produce repositories nobody can run. Teach the criterion (small ·
synthetic or public · needed to run the code) rather than the slogan.

## The example repo uses merge commits on purpose

The handout tells students to **Squash and merge**. The example repository
itself uses merge commits, and Part 3 now has a collapsed note explaining why:
squashing would flatten away the branch topology that the repository exists to
demonstrate.

Do not "fix" this later. If you ever rebuild the example repo, keep merge
commits, and keep recommending squash for student projects. The two-sentence
version for class: *squashing makes history readable, which is what you want;
it also makes branching invisible, which is what we need to look at today.*

The graph is worth putting on a slide as-is. Read bottom to top it contains a
clean PR, a shared-branch conflict, a stale PR, and a conflict resolved inside
a branch — all four situations students will meet, in one picture.

## Things students reliably get wrong

| Mistake | Why it happens | Pre-empt it by |
|---|---|---|
| Not pulling before working | Nothing visibly breaks until it does | Making "look at the Git pane arrows" a ritual |
| Forgetting local `main` after a merge | GitHub shows merged; their laptop doesn't move | Showing `git branch -vv` before and after |
| Committing `.RData` / rendered HTML | RStudio creates them silently | `.gitignore` before the first commit |
| Project inside Dropbox/OneDrive | It is where their coursework already lives | Saying it out loud in Part 2, with the reason |
| `--force` after a rejected push | It is the top Stack Overflow answer | Naming it explicitly as forbidden, and why |
| Merging their own PR | It is one click | Grading it |

## On letting AI do the git work

The design assumption is that students delegate mechanics and own meaning. It
holds up as long as they have the model from Part 1. Without it, an AI-driven
student will resolve a conflict by accepting whichever version the model liked,
and never notice that a teammate's paragraph vanished.

So the napkin check is the real gate, not the walkthrough. If a student cannot
draw the four places, more practice with prompts will not help them.

## Assessment suggestions

Grade the repository, not just the report:

- **Process (visible in the history)** — commits small and frequent; messages
  explain why; every contribution merged via a PR someone else approved;
  `main` renders from a fresh clone.
- **Hygiene** — no data over ~1 MB, no secrets, `.gitignore` present from the
  first commit.
- **Contribution** — `git shortlog -sn` shows who committed what. Useful for
  detecting the group where one person did everything; do not use it
  mechanically, since pair programming and reviewing are real work that shows
  up as few commits.

A good single exam question: *"Your teammate pushed work you don't have, and
your push was rejected. Explain what happened and what you will do — and what
would happen if you used `--force`."*

## The Dropbox warning is not theoretical

While these pages were being written — inside a Dropbox folder — Dropbox
created **18 "conflicted copy" files** in the render output and replaced
`_site/index.html` with a 253-byte redirect stub. The site silently served a
broken page with every stylesheet and script 404ing.

Nothing was lost, because the corruption hit only the disposable `_site/`
output and not the `.qmd` sources. But it is a clean demonstration of the point
Part 2 makes to students: a sync client and a build tool both writing to the
same directory will eventually collide.

Two fixes, in order of preference:

1. **Keep projects out of synced folders.** `~/projects`, not Dropbox.
2. If a project must live in Dropbox, mark the build output as Dropbox-ignored
   *before* rendering:

```bash
mkdir -p _site .quarto
xattr -w com.dropbox.ignored 1 _site
xattr -w com.dropbox.ignored 1 .quarto
```

Applied to the old Dropbox copy, this took the conflicted-copy count from 18
to zero across three consecutive renders. It did **not** eliminate the problem
entirely — one further render still failed with

``` text
ERROR: NotFound: No such file or directory (os error 2): rename ...
```

which succeeded on a plain retry. So treat it as a mitigation that makes a
folder usable, not a cure. It protects the output directory only; it does
nothing for a `.git` directory. **Do not rely on it to make a git repository
safe inside Dropbox.**

In the end this tutorial and its example project were both moved out to
`~/projects/`, which is what Part 2 tells students to do. Three renders in the
new location: no errors, no conflicted copies. If you are going to ask students
to keep projects out of synced folders, the course materials should not be
sitting in one.

## Maintaining this tutorial

Every command and output in these pages was executed on macOS with git 2.39.3,
gh 2.90.0, R 4.6.0 and Quarto 1.4.554. The Windows and Linux install
instructions were **not** tested — verify them once on a student machine before
first use.

Re-render after editing:

```bash
quarto render
```
